activities.anchor: the full span of a life, not merely the hospital ward
activities.caption: file each occupation by its family
activities.name: otFamilySort

config.prompt: The occupation families — file each activity:

items.label: using transport, taking medications correctly, shopping
play and leisure, social participation, rest and sleep

config.why: Two properties make any of these an occupation rather than a mere task: it is personally meaningful, and it holds a place in roles and routines.

activities.anchor: Refugees who cannot work in their host country
activities.caption: drag between the assumption and the dark mirror
activities.name: otDepriveCompare

config.prompt: Drag across the claim that proves the construct's power:

before.label: the assumption
before.text: Meaningful occupation is a pleasant extra — nice to have, first thing cut in hospitals, prisons and institutions.

after.label: the dark mirror
after.text: Wherever doing is stripped out — confinement without structure, institutions without cooking or gardens — mood, identity, skill and health decline, independent of physical condition.

config.why: That observation scales into occupational justice — and it is why the profession's remit stretches from an ICU bedside to housing policy.

activities.anchor: A delivery driver with lower-back pain can be strengthened
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the CMOP-E note
activities.name: otCmopSpot

config.prompt: One line of this model summary is wrong — click it:
lines: CMOP-E pictures a person — cognitive, affective and physical around a spiritual core — at the centre of occupation.
Self-care, productivity and leisure sit nested inside cultural, institutional, physical and social environments.
Dysfunction is a fixed property of the person — the diagnosis decides what therapy can achieve.
The transverse strip where person, occupation and world intersect is occupational performance and engagement.
Strengthen the person, re-teach the task, or re-equip the environment — three legitimate routes for one problem.
config.correction: Dysfunction is not a property of the person alone but of the person–environment–occupation mismatch — workable from any of the three corners.
config.why: The fit idea is the model's signature contribution — and the COPM exists to elicit the client's own priorities for it.

activities.anchor: Both push the therapist away from the impairment obsession that medical settings breed
activities.caption: drag between the two models' questions
activities.name: otModelsCompare

config.prompt: Drag across the field's two shared lenses:

before.label: MOHO — why does this person not do?
before.text: Volition (the motivation to act), habituation (habits and internalised roles), performance capacity (what body and mind deliver moment to moment) — three different problems, three different therapies.

after.label: CMOP-E — where is the mismatch?
after.text: Person, occupation, environment: the intersection where dysfunction lives, relieved from any corner by fit, evidence and the client's priorities.

config.why: The WHO's ICF gave the wider health system a vocabulary for exactly this shift — functioning and participation in context.

activities.anchor: Good OT does both, and knows which it is doing
activities.caption: sequence the analysis-to-intervention moves
activities.name: otAnalysisOrder

config.prompt: From task to treatment, in order:
items: Dissect the occupation into demands: objects, sequence and timing, body functions, social and safety layers
Compare the demand structure to this client's capacities
Grade — scale the demand: a 300 ml kettle, tea made seated, then standing, then carrying the tray
Adapt — change the task or tools: a flip-top lid, a jar opener, the kettle on the counter
config.why: Adaptation restores the occupation today while graded challenge rebuilds capacity for tomorrow — two moves aimed at two horizons.

activities.anchor: A therapist who treats every aid as defeat
activities.caption: true or false — aids, grading and goals
activities.name: otAidJudge

statements.s: Restoring unaided movement is always the real goal.
statements.why: That confuses the means (grip, range) with the end — the life the client wants back.

statements.s: Adaptation and grading aim at two different horizons — today's occupation and tomorrow's capacity.
statements.why: Two tools, and good practice knows which one it is using.

statements.s: For many clients the honest clinical answer is to change the environment rather than the body.
statements.why: The mismatch can be relieved from any corner — including the world around the person.

statements.s: Using exercise as one tool among many means therapy has failed.
statements.why: Exercise is one tool in service of the occupation — never the goal itself.

activities.anchor: This is what lets one profession treat a child with cerebral palsy
activities.caption: walk the two-teas problem
activities.name: otTeaBranch

config.root: Two clients both 'make tea'. Walk why the analysis is never generic.

start.text: The standard demand structure of tea-making is known. What must happen next?

choices.label: Re-run the analysis for this client — kitchen, habits, meaning
Apply the textbook demands — the task is the task

generic.text: The textbook demands miss this client's kitchen, habits and meaning — activity analysis is generic, occupational analysis is personal.

personal.text: And the analysis runs both directions. Forward finds where a stroke survivor's neglect breaks the chain — the forgotten milk, the scalded hand.

backward.text: Backward designs occupations that train the deficit — dough-kneading chosen precisely because it loads bilateral hand use, standing tolerance and sequencing at once.

config.why: One profession, three clients — the method generalises because occupations are chosen and tuned against an analysed demand structure.

activities.anchor: the same diagnosis lands in utterly different lives
activities.caption: bet before you read on — where goals come from
activities.name: otGoalPredict

config.q: A stroke protocol exists. Where do this patient's therapy goals come from?
choices: From the diagnosis — the stroke determines the goals
From the occupational profile: who this person is and what they need and want to do
From the therapist's standard stroke programme
From the hospital's average outcome data
config.why: The baker's arm and the chess player's arm are the same lesion in different lives — goals written as occupations and scored on the client's own ratings are the construct's audit trail.
